title: U.S. Mortgage Rates Hit Highest Level in Over a Year as Iran Conflict Keeps Inflation Elevated
excerpt: The 30-year fixed rate reached 6.66%, driving pending home sales to a three-month low, but falling asking prices offer an opening for buyers willing to negotiate.
body:
• The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 6.66% this week, the highest since July 2025, according to Freddie Mac, with the daily average touching 6.85%.
  • U.S. pending home sales fell to their lowest level since early April, dropping 1.7% in the last week alone, per Redfin data.
  • Rising oil prices tied to the Iran conflict and stubborn inflation are keeping rates elevated, with the PCE price index still at 3.7% annually — well above the Fed's 2% target.
  • The median U.S. housing payment fell to $2,575, a three-month low, as sellers cut asking prices to their lowest level in a year.

U.S. mortgage rates surged to their highest level in more than a year last week, driven by inflation fears tied to the Middle East conflict, and the housing market is showing the strain.

Rates Climb as Iran War Fuels Inflation

The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.66% for the week ending July 30, the highest reading since July 2025, according to Freddie Mac. The daily average rate pushed even higher, touching 6.85% by late last week, per Mortgage News Daily.

The catalyst is clear: five months into U.S. and Israeli military operations in Iran, restricted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have kept energy prices elevated and inflation sticky. The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index dropped 0.1% from May in June — a brief reprieve during a Middle East truce — but the annual rate remains at 3.7%, nearly double the Federal Reserve's 2% target, according to CNN.

"Oil and inflation remain the biggest drivers, and mortgage rates will likely need energy prices to settle and inflation to remain under control before they can move meaningfully lower."

— Jeff DerGurahian, Head Economist, loanDepot

Demand Falls Below Year-Ago Levels

The rate spike is cooling buyer activity. U.S. pending home sales fell to their lowest level since early April during the four weeks ending July 26, dropping 1.7% in the final week alone, according to a Redfin report published on BusinessWire. Mortgage-purchase applications fell 4% week over week, per the Mortgage Bankers Association, while refinance applications plunged 10%.

Home tours are up just 15% from the start of 2026, compared with a 31% increase at the same point last year, ShowingTime data shows — a sign that buyer enthusiasm is fading even as inventory grows.

Bright Spots for Buyers

There is a silver lining. Sellers are adjusting to weaker demand. The median asking price dropped to its lowest level in a year, pulling the median U.S. housing payment down to $2,575 — a three-month low, despite elevated rates. The median sale price sits at $407,752, roughly $2,000 shy of the record high, according to Redfin.

Crucially, there are hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers in the market. That imbalance gives those who can afford to buy real negotiating leverage.

"Rates are higher now, but bidding wars are unlikely and buyers are often able to negotiate prices down and get concessions from sellers," said Bonnie Phillips, a Redfin Premier agent in Cleveland. "Today's housing market rewards patience over panic."

What the Fed Is Signaling

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate steady this week, but Chairman Kevin Warsh's comments offered little comfort to rate-sensitive buyers. Warsh suggested rising Treasury yields may be "partially doing the Fed's job" of taming inflation by raising borrowing costs across the economy, according to CNN.

Some economists are more hawkish. Capital Economics expects the RBI-equivalent repo rate hikes of 75 basis points over the coming months if oil pressures persist. At BofA Global Research, Rahul Bajoria expects any tightening to begin no earlier than December.

What It Means for Indian-American Homebuyers

Indian Americans are among the most active homebuyer demographics in the U.S., with particularly high ownership rates in tech hubs like the San Francisco Bay Area, Seattle, and the New York metro. Higher rates disproportionately affect first-time buyers — many of them younger H-1B professionals — who lack the equity cushion to absorb elevated monthly payments.

For those considering a purchase, the current dynamic offers a tradeoff: higher borrowing costs, but less competition and greater room to negotiate on price.

What's Next

Rates will remain hostage to geopolitics. Any sustained resolution to the Iran conflict that stabilizes oil prices could bring mortgage rates back below 6%, where they briefly dipped earlier this year. Without that, the consensus among 21 forecasters tracked by ResiClub puts the average 30-year rate at 6.18% for 2026 — suggesting little relief ahead.
